Copies of the staff reports or other written documentation relating to each item of business referred to
on the agenda are on file in the office of the City Clerk and are available for public inspection. If
applicable, materials related to an item on this agenda submitted to the Council after distribution of the
agenda packet are available for public inspection in the City Clerk’s office during normal business
hours. Any person having any question concerning any agenda item may call the City Clerk to make
inquiry concerning the item. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the agenda packet can be
made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability in compliance with the
Americans with Disabilities Act. Please contact the City Clerk at 310-378-0383, at least 48 hours
prior to the meeting to request a disability-related modification or accommodation.

The City Council welcomes and encourages public participation at the Council meetings; however,
to allow for the orderly progression of business, each person wishing to comment or make a
presentation shall be limited to three (3) minutes. Anyone wishing to address the City Council shall
fill out a green speaker’s card available at the end of each row in the Chambers. The card permits
the City to identify persons for purposes of City Council minute preparation. Please see specific
agenda sections below for any other requirements related to meeting participation. The City
Council, at the direction of the Mayor with concurrence of the Council, may modify the order of
items shown on the agenda.

A regular meeting of the City Council of the City of Palos Verdes Estates was called to order
this day at 7:30 PM in the Council Chambers of City Hall by Mayor Bird.

  Treasurer Sherwood, City Attorney Hogin, Asst. to City Manager Davis,

CEREMONIAL MATTERS

    SWEARING-IN OF POLICE OFFICER CHARLOTTE SIMON

Chief Dreiling introduced Police Officer Charlotte Simon. Officer Simon graduated from Fullerton
Police Academy in June 2011, and has recently completed in-house field training with flying
colors. Chief Dreiling administered the Oath of Office. Officer Simon’s grandmother pinned on
her badge with a prayer. Officer Simon introduced her family, friends, and academy classmates.
Council and staff congratulated Officer Simon.

 District representative introduced District & Vector-Borne Disease Control District Executive
 Director Bob Saviskas, (PowerPoint), who provided an operations outline of the District, which
 was established in 1924; it serves 4.2 million people and is second largest vector control in CA by
 population. Vector insect programs cover: mosquito controls, Africanized honey bees, stinging
 insect control, lyme disease-causing ticks, and fire ants. He reported that lyme disease carrying

Robert Jystad, RPV, VP of California Wireless Association, said they promote relationships with

pivotal role played by telecommunicators, who provide support services to first responders in
emergencies. He said 70% of 911 calls come from wireless devices, and that investments in

10.  AWARD OF THE RESIDENTIAL REFUSE AND RECYCLING COLLECTION
  CONTRACT BEGINNING JULY 1, 2012

 Director Rigg reported that the current refuse collection contract expires on June 30, 2012. Athens
CITY COUNCIL
April 10, 2012

  3
  Services has provided service since 2007 when they obtained the franchise from Norcal. The
 existing scope of service has been the same for many years, with backyard trash picked up weekly
 and recyclables picked up every other week. City Council reviewed and modified the contract
 specifications at their meeting of September 13, 2011, including awarding a contract based on
 value. Three companies responded to the RFP. He corrected Alternate 2 quote by CDS on the staff
 report to $43.21.

 Director Rigg explained the current 3-barrel system. He said the 2-barrel system is a new
 alternative, which includes refuse and recyclables comingled in the same container; then separated
 at a recycling facility to achieve higher diversion rates. He said this would result in less of a
 burden on residents, as well as one less collection vehicle on the street. During a test conducted a
 year ago of random samplings in the City, Director Rigg said it was found that 50% of the weight
 of the materials collected could have been recycled.

 Director Rigg said three service options were quoted by each hauler, including (Alternative 1)
 weekly collection (3-barrel system); (Alternative 2) weekly collection with recyclables collected
 every other week; and (Alternative 3) weekly collection with recycles and refuse comingled (2-
 barrel system). He said the cities of San Marino and South Pasadena also have rear yard service
 provided by Athens. Each hauler was checked for provision of rear yard service references. All
 vendors were rated very good, with 4.6 to 4.89 range in overall performance. He said two of the
 bidders offered a variety of additional services at no additional cost, ranging from street sweeping
 to shredding, curbside pickup of sharps and e-waste.

 Councilmember Rea confirmed with staff that the overall current diversion rate is ~60%, which has
 increased slightly over time. Councilmember Rea asked if we had any feedback from San Marino
 or South Pasadena regarding their experience with the 2-barrel system with backyard pick-up.
 Director Rigg responded that both rated Athens very high; South Pasadena is happy with the 2-
 barrel system.

 Councilmember Humphrey asked about EDCO’s experience with RPV. Director Rigg said they
 service a limited amount of residents in the City with a rear yard option; cans are brought to the
 street by the hauler and then dumped mechanically. But in PVE, they would empty green waste
 into a tote, then it would be taken to the truck at the street.

 Councilmember Perkins asked about our experience with Athens. Director Rigg said we’ve
 received very few complaints about Athens service. Councilmember Perkins about how diversion
 rates might increase by changing from a 3 to 2-barrel system. Director Rigg said South Pasadena, a
 similar community using the 2-barrel system, increased their diversion rate to 67%, and he hoped
 we would also get into the high 60's with this system.

 Samuel Pena, (Republic Services, Inc.) Consolidated Disposal Service, said they service Rolling
 Hills with the 2-barrel system twice a week with back and side yard service, which is similar in
 fashion to what is proposed in Alternate 3. They have more than 30 customers in L.A. County,
 including Hawthorne, Lawndale, El Segundo, Hermosa Beach, with Inglewood just awarded. He
 said Alternate 3, with mixed processing is a pretty clean stream; they changed Rolling Hills from 3
 to the 2 barrel system and increased diversion from 55% to ~70% and they offer them brush
CITY COUNCIL
April 10, 2012

  4
  clearing, bulky item days, recycling events, unlimited free bulky and twice weekly pick-ups.

 Steve South, EDCO, President/CEO, family owned and operated since 1967; he introduced key
 personnel. He said the Proposal recognized significant transitional experience - RPV and La
 Mirada. He said their sister company Burrtec Waste and Recycling has significant backyard
 experience in the Coachella Valley, including Rancho Mirage, with a backyard approach similar to
 this proposal. For Alt. 1, EDCO projects a 70% diversion level and weekly recycling will
 significantly improve participation. They also advocate SERF (diversion credit); with Alt. 2, they
 project 65% diversion rate. He said public education is a key component to any provider.

 Gary Clifford, Athens Services, asked to continue their long relationship with the City. Athens
 significant backyard experience in the industry and effectively removing waste on scene in rear
 load vehicles provide diminimus impact on the environment. He said PVE is a specialty they've
 honed and they have included numerous enhancements to current service levels. New back loader
 trucks will minimize waste. He said they offer street sweeping and other educational opportunities,
 and a 70% diversion rate with Alt. 3 is projected. He concluded their customer service excellence
 has been codified, and they are offering added services.

 MPT Goodhart thanked the three companies represented this evening. He said this is a value-based
 award; cost is not the most important criteria, noting that the difference in rates quoted range from
 an additional ~$30-$50 annually, although one objective is to keep the cost as low as possible.
 Excellent service is more important. Each company has some rear yard experience; Athens has an
 excellent record and the other firms also have good recommendations as well. He opined waste
 diversion will never go lower; 60% is the minimum, and maximizing diversion is important. He
 opined that the Alt. 3/ 2-barrel system would provide the fewest number of trucks in our city and is
 the best approach. All bidding firms have good waste recovery facilities, noting that Athens is not
 at close as the other companies. He said safety records are important; no complete picture was
 provided on the OSHA form. He did not consider street sweeping and other added services offered
 in his assessment. All proposals were responsive, but he would have liked more information from
 CDS.

 Councilmember Humphrey said she hadn’t considered these added services either and based her
 assessment on who would provide the best service and value for our residents. She agreed that
 diversion rates would be increase with Alternative 3/weekly collection, recalling a video
 presentation of MRF (Material Recovery Facility) showing manual and mechanical separation of
 recyclables. She said the three firms were responsive with good references. She said consideration
 of the service currently provided by our current hauler was part of her consideration, and she
 favored Alternate 3 when they award the contract.

 Councilmember Rea said he also favored Alternate 3. It is exciting to go to a 2-barrel system
 resulting in increased diversion rates and convenience to our citizens, providing less burden to our
 residents sorting garbage. The transition would be awkward at first, but a time saving relief for our
 citizens. He also supported weekly pick-up. He said the low bidder for this alternate is Athens and
 noted that the City has been pleased with the quality of their service. He said Council’s decision to
 request proposals did not reflect negatively upon them, but to explore other approaches. He said
 there is ~$1/month savings and he supported awarding Alternate 3 to Athens Services. He said he
CITY COUNCIL
April 10, 2012

  5
  had not considered extras or alternatives because they were not part of the contract RFP.

 Councilmember Perkins said during this process it became clear they had an opportunity to insure
 the best service to our residents, and we are well positioned for the future--increasing diversion
 rates to maximum extent possible and providing benefit to our residents. She was pleased to see
 that all 3 bidders had good customer service records. She had not taken into account the
 enhancements proposed, which is not the basis for this award. She concurred with Council in her
 support of Alt. 3/2-barrel system. She said it seemed counter intuitive that not separating trash
 would increase diversion, but is now convinced this is the way we should go. She said they have
 been pleased with Athens service, noting sometimes unforeseen things can happen in any
 transition. Given the quality of service with Athens, she supported awarding Alternate 3 to Athens.

 Mayor Bird thanked all three providers and said they are making their decision based on the
 materials submitted in response to the RFP, although he appreciated that other services are
 available. He disagreed with using Alt. 3 because we need to do a better job of recycling education.
 He opined that going to a 2 barrel system sends a message that we will pay for service to separate
 trash when we could be doing that in our homes; it is a missed opportunity. The fact that we are
 not doing as well as we could [with diversion] provides an opportunity for education. It is $2 less
 per month to have a 3-barrel system, which is another incentive for our residents to keep our
 current system in place. He opined collection of recyclables every other week is satisfactory; he
 favored Alternative 2. He said natural gas vehicles would provide no added pollution with an extra
 truck on the street. He appreciated the current service level and this process has reinforced the job
 Athens has done for the City. He supported an award to Athens with Alternate 2.

 Councilmember Humphrey was not sure increased education would accomplish additional
 diversion. She, herself, worked hard at recycling, but in the long run, she felt better diversion could
 be done by people with greater training and expertise.

 Councilmember Rea’s view was that we have been educated for decades about recycling; he did
 not know how much more would help. For a smaller margin return, we may have reached a plateau.
 It would take a lot more education to achieve a high rate of diversion. He supported the two barrel
 approach.

 Councilmember Perkins also agreed diversion drove her decision. She believed it would be hard to
 increase diversion without doing something significant; we will be under pressure to increase
 diversion with landfills closing.

 MPT Goodhart said he was educated about recycling, with good practices in place. But, he was
 shocked at how much additional material could be recycled when he saw the results of the test,
 opining that you can only educate to a certain extent. Diversion is most important at the end of the
 day.

 Councilmember Humphrey said she supported Alternate 3 and educating residents about the
 changes that will occur. She asked Director Rigg if mixing food products in with green waste is
 part of Alt. 3. Director Rigg said he would like the Council to specify what they wish to include
 within the contract award. The food waste program is an additional service offered; it can be added
CITY COUNCIL
April 10, 2012

  6
  to the contract, or Council can specify to include the "list of additional services". It is available
 from Athens with any of the alternatives awarded.

 Councilmember Rea asked staff what other services had been offered by Athens. Director Rigg
 said Attachment F of the staff report included a variety of additional services offered. Athens
 formalized the offer within Attachment F; EDCO included them within their proposal. But he
 understood award should not be based on these features, but recommended consideration because
 of their value and he liked the other items offered within Attachment F. Councilmember Rea said
 this was not part of his decision process, but would not wish to turn those services away and would
 want them to be made part of the award. Director Rigg said curbside composting is part of food
 waste option.

 Councilmember Humphrey said continued sidewalk cleaning was not considered as an add-on
 option from Athens. Director Rigg said they've done a variety of free services, but they were not
 required to do them. He recommended that they should be included within the award.

 MPT Goodhart asked if all items would be listed within contract - optional programs included. He
 said a lot of residents do compost and he does not put meat in his compost waste; he was not sure
 of the value this provides.

 Councilmember Humphrey said she does not compost, but this method would be a good way to
 segue into doing this.

 Councilmember Perkins agreed there is waste that is being reused and not composted. Mayor Bird
 said it appears Council has consensus to go to a 2-barrel system and award the contract to Athens in
 accordance to Attachment F.

 On motion of Councilmember Rea, seconded by Councilmember Perkins, Council approved the
 Award of the Residential Refuse and Recycling Collection Contract to Athens Services for
 Alternate 3, which is to include the 3 page summary of additional services provided by Athens
 Services in Attachment F of the written staff report, beginning July 1, 2012, by unanimous oral
 vote.

STAFF REPORTS

11.  CITY MANAGER'S REPORT

 City Manager Smith asked Chief Dreiling to introduce new Community Relations Officer Marcelle
 McCullough.

 Chief Dreiling said Marcelle McCullough is devoted to community disaster preparedness and is a
 certified CERT Trainer. In 2008, she helped Redondo Beach with its California Shake Out Drill,
 and facilitated the AES Plant drill in 2010. In 2011, she worked with the City of Manhattan Beach
 with their Shakeout drill. CRO McCullough also assisted RPV equip their three emergency cache
 containers and consulted, as a volunteer, with PVE when equipping our own 6 DDP containers.
CITY COUNCIL
April 10, 2012

  7
  Marcelle also has experience as an event organizer, and he welcomed Ms. McCullough to the City.

 Councilmember Rea asked Ms. McCullough about CERT training and its lengthy courses. Ms.
 McCullough said CERT is a FEMA program with 20 hours required training. She said she was
 excited to be with the City and serving the PVE community.

 City Manager Smith reported that this evening's agenda was implemented utilizing new software
 provided by SIRE Technologies, which also provides for the ability for Deputy City Clerk
 Kroneberger to take live minutes during the meeting, integrating with digital audio capability that
 will be uploaded to City website. She introduced software code writer and trainer Alma Ohene-
 Opare of SIRE.

 Councilmember Goodhart asked City Manager Smith to describe how this will benefit our
 residents. City Manager Smith explained that Council Agenda packets, in their entirety, are now
 available to residents on the City’s website, including staff reports with supporting attachments.
 Additionally, a resident may listen to an item of interest by clicking on that agenda, which links
 them directly to the corresponding audio recording, greatly enhancing transparency.

 Mr. Ohene-Opare said one can listen via Media Player on their computers with the ability to stop,
 rewind, and fast forward as desired.

 Mayor Bird confirmed with City Manager Smith that video is not included with this service at this
 time.
